premise: Four college friends rehearse a production of Romeo and Juliet while their own loves and infidelities play out offstage, the play's doomed romance running alongside messier real ones. Flanagan made this coming-of-age drama as a student feature at Towson University in Maryland, writing, directing, editing and scoring it himself, and it was billed as an independent digital feature on its 2000 release. There is no horror here and no ghost in the frame, yet the shape is already familiar: a small group of friends, a story staged inside the story, and people slowly working out the truth about each other. The film has never had a public release. TMDB lists it as not currently known to be available for viewing, so it survives as a line in his filmography and a short cast list.
whyItMatters: Makebelieve is the first entry in the Flanagan filmography and the first place he did every job at once. He wrote, directed, edited and composed it, and editing his own work stayed a constant: he still cuts his features and many of his series episodes. The device of characters staging a story while living one comes back, far darker, in The Midnight Club, where dying teenagers tell tales at midnight. Two of its actors, Jamie Sinsz and Zak Jeffries, reappear in Ghosts of Hamilton Street three years later, the earliest sign of his habit of reassembling a cast.
trivia: Flanagan is credited as director, writer, editor and composer.
The story follows four college friends during a production of Romeo and Juliet.
TMDB notes the film is not currently known to be publicly available.
Jamie Sinsz and Zak Jeffries act in both Makebelieve and Ghosts of Hamilton Street.
A second student feature, Still Life (2001), followed; it has no TMDB entry.

premise: Brody Campbell, a troubled writer, notices the people in his life vanishing one by one, and nobody else seems to register that they were ever there. Each disappearance drops him into a version of the world where that person never existed, so the first suspect is his own sanity. Once he works out that the vanishings follow a specific order, the film turns from paranoia into a rescue story: he has to get ahead of the pattern and save the people he loves from forces he may never understand. Flanagan wrote, directed and edited this third student feature in 2003, and TMDB bills it as award-winning. Like the earlier features it is not publicly available, which makes its premise one of the more tantalising lost items in his catalog.
whyItMatters: Grief by subtraction is the engine here: a man losing people and having to prove they existed. That fear drives Absentia eight years later, where a husband is about to be declared dead after vanishing, and it runs through much of what Flanagan has made since. The film also starts his collaboration with Scott Graham, who plays Brody and then anchors Oculus: Chapter 3 before turning up in Absentia and Oculus. Jamie Sinsz and Zak Jeffries return from Makebelieve, so the repertory instinct was in place before Flanagan had a professional credit.
trivia: Scott Graham plays the lead, Brody Campbell, and stars in Oculus: Chapter 3 three years later.
The tagline asks: What if everyone you love disappeared, and you were the only one who noticed?
TMDB describes it as an award-winning student film.
Flanagan is credited as director, writer and editor.
The film is not currently known to be publicly available.

premise: A man locks himself in a room with an antique mirror, a bank of cameras and a set of safeguards, determined to prove on tape that the mirror is haunted and that it kills. Flanagan made the 32-minute short for $1,500 as one chapter of a planned series about the mirror; when financing for the series fell through, he shot this chapter on its own to show he could direct horror. Scott Graham carries it as Tim Russel, the man running the experiment. The structure is the seed of everything that followed: the cameras, the timers, the obsessive logging of each strange event, and the creeping sense that the mirror is running the test, not the man. The short did well enough on the festival circuit that it became the 2013 feature.
whyItMatters: This is where the Lasser Glass starts, even if the first mirror was a plastic “Monte Paraiso” model bought online. The feature built a new mirror, and that frame has since hidden in Ouija: Origin of Evil, Doctor Sleep, Midnight Mass and The Midnight Club, and become the headboard in Gerald's Game. The short also opened the door to the partnership that made the feature possible: its festival life led to Oculus with Trevor Macy and Intrepid Pictures, the start of more than a decade of producing together.
trivia: The short cost $1,500 to make.
It was planned as one chapter in a series of mirror shorts; Flanagan made it alone when financing fell through.
The mirror was a plastic “Monte Paraiso” model bought online.
Sources disagree on the year: Wikipedia's Oculus article says 2005, while the filmography table and TMDB say 2006.
TMDB credits Flanagan himself as “Ghoul 2.”
Its festival popularity led directly to the feature Oculus.

premise: Tricia's husband Daniel has been missing for seven years, and she is finally about to have him declared dead in absentia. Her younger sister Callie, a recovering addict, moves in to help and soon has a strange encounter in the pedestrian tunnel near the house. Then Daniel reappears, emaciated and traumatised. The tunnel turns out to be the lair of an unseen, insect-like thing that has been taking people for decades, and it is not finished with this family. Flanagan keeps the creature out of sight and lets the dread come from the sisters: one still holding out hope, the other urging her to let go. The ending takes Daniel again, then Tricia, then Callie herself, and refuses to soften any of it.
whyItMatters: Absentia is the first Flanagan feature most people can actually watch, and the place the repertory begins. Katie Parker, who plays Callie, is the actor who has been with him longest, and Courtney Bell, Doug Jones and Flanagan's sibling Jamie are all here too. It introduced his signature subject, grief and the people left behind, in its most literal form: a wife with no body to bury. It also proved that a $70,000 Kickstarter film could carry him to the next step, which turned out to be Oculus with Trevor Macy.
trivia: Made for $70,000, with principal photography funded through Kickstarter.
Premiered March 3, 2011, at the Fargo Film Festival, then won Best Feature at Maelstrom and Best Horror Feature at Shriekfest.
Flanagan lived across the street from the real tunnel used in the film.
He has said it was subconsciously inspired by the 1983 Fraggle Rock episode “The Terrible Tunnel.”
Doug Jones plays Walter Lambert, and Flanagan's sibling, credited as James, plays Jamie Lambert.
Phase 4 Films handled the North American DVD and VOD release.

sourceMaterial.author: Mike Flanagan
sourceMaterial.title: Oculus: Chapter 3 – The Man with the Plan
sourceMaterial.note: Expanded from his own short, adding the siblings and the childhood timeline around the original experiment.

premise: Tim Russell is released at 21 from the psychiatric hospital where he was held after shooting his father as a boy. His sister Kaylie has spent those years tracking down the Lasser Glass, the antique mirror she blames for their parents' deaths, and she has a plan: a room full of cameras, timers and a weighted anchor rigged as a kill switch, to prove the mirror's power and then destroy it. The film braids that one night with the siblings' childhood, and the cuts get slipperier as the mirror leaves both of them unsure which timeline they are standing in. It ends with Tim tricked into triggering the anchor that kills Kaylie, then arrested, repeating the past exactly. It is a haunted-object movie built like a family tragedy.
whyItMatters: Oculus is where the core crew assembles: Michael Fimognari behind the camera, The Newton Brothers on the score, Jeff Howard as co-writer, Trevor Macy producing, and Kate Siegel in a small part as Marisol Chavez. Its braided past-and-present structure is the template Flanagan later stretched across ten episodes; he has called Hill House “a 10-hour Oculus.” The Lasser Glass became his most famous recurring prop, hidden in at least five later works. Karen Gillan, Annalise Basso and Katee Sackhoff all came back years later, in The Life of Chuck and Carrie.
trivia: Made for about $5 million; it grossed about $44 million worldwide.
Flanagan has said it began as a riff on Stephen King's “1408,” and he pitched the mirror as a “portable Overlook Hotel.”
Bruce Larsen designed the Lasser Glass, and later the Hush mask and Before I Wake's Canker Man.
Premiered at TIFF in September 2013 and opened in the US on April 11, 2014.
Flanagan keeps hiding the mirror in later work partly to keep the mythology alive for a possible follow-up, stalled by murky rights after Relativity's bankruptcy.
An Indian remake, Dobaara: See Your Evil (2017), carries Flanagan's story credit.

premise: Jessie and Mark Hobson, still grieving the son who drowned in the bath, foster eight-year-old Cody, a boy who is terrified of falling asleep. They soon learn why: while he sleeps, his dreams become real. Butterflies fill the house, then their dead son appears, and Jessie starts using Cody to see him again. Nightmares come true as well, and Cody's produce the Canker Man, a figure that consumes people, eventually including Mark. The answer is grief seen from the other side: the Canker Man is Cody's warped memory of his mother dying of cancer. Jessie adopts him and helps him face it, which makes this the gentlest of Flanagan's early films and one of the saddest.
whyItMatters: Before I Wake puts a child at the center of the supernatural, with Jacob Tremblay, who came back for Doctor Sleep and The Life of Chuck. It started Annabeth Gish's run, and it holds a design secret: Bruce Larsen's mold for the Canker Man became the killer's mask in Hush, released the same year. Its theme, a parent using the uncanny to hold on to a dead child, is a quieter rehearsal for what Hill House would do with a whole family. It is also the only Flanagan score Danny Elfman shared with The Newton Brothers.
trivia: Relativity Media set four release dates and never released it; the company's bankruptcy left it on the shelf.
Released as Somnia in some territories.
It reached Netflix outside the US in April 2017 and Netflix US on January 5, 2018.
Danny Elfman shares the score credit with The Newton Brothers.
Flanagan has confirmed the Hush mask was made from Bruce Larsen's mold of the Canker Man's face.
Jacob Tremblay plays Cody, the first of his three Flanagan roles.

premise: Maddie Young, a deaf and mute horror novelist living alone in the woods, is working through endings for her next book when a masked man with a crossbow kills her neighbour Sarah on her doorstep. Because Maddie cannot hear him, he decides to toy with her rather than finish the job, and the film becomes a tight, near-wordless game of cat and mouse around one house. Flanagan and Kate Siegel, who co-wrote it and plays Maddie, build the suspense out of what she can see and what we can hear, and the turn comes when she stops reacting and starts plotting like one of her own characters. She survives and kills him with a corkscrew. At about 80 minutes, it is his leanest feature.
whyItMatters: Hush is the first Flanagan film written with Kate Siegel, whom he married the same year, and the first to land on Netflix, the home that would carry his series for seven years. It brought Samantha Sloyan and Michael Trucco into the company, and John Gallagher Jr., the masked man, returns a decade later in The Exorcist: Martyrs. It also hides the longest setup of his career: the novel on Maddie's screen is Midnight Mass, with Riley and Crockett island named on the back cover, five years before the series existed.
trivia: Netflix bought worldwide rights before the SXSW premiere on March 12, 2016; it streamed from April 8.
Maddie's novel is Midnight Mass, and the on-screen text comes from Flanagan's real unpublished manuscript.
Maddie's inner voice weighs an ending: “Erin dies. Can't kill Erin.”
The mask was built from Bruce Larsen's Canker Man mold for Before I Wake, and was not modelled on Kate Siegel's face.
Shot in Alabama; the script was first blocked out in Flanagan and Siegel's own house.
Samantha Sloyan plays Sarah Greene; Kate Siegel later plays Erin Greene in Midnight Mass.
A partygoer wears the mask in Usher's “The Masque of the Red Death.”

sourceMaterial.author: Hasbro
sourceMaterial.title: Ouija (board game) and Ouija (2014)
sourceMaterial.note: A prequel to the 2014 film, with an original 1967 story by Flanagan and Jeff Howard built around the board.

premise: Los Angeles, 1967. Widowed Alice Zander runs a fake séance business with her daughters Lina and Doris, and adds a Ouija board to the act as a prop. Then young Doris starts making genuine contact. The voices she channels belong to people a doctor once held and experimented on in a secret room hidden in the house, and they are using her to act. Flanagan and Jeff Howard play the early scenes as a warm, slightly shabby family story, so the possession lands as a loss rather than a stunt, and Lulu Wilson's Doris gives the film its lasting image. Father Tom and Alice are killed and Lina ends up institutionalised, which hands the story over to the 2014 film it precedes, with Lin Shaye as the older Lina in a post-credits scene.
whyItMatters: Ouija showed Flanagan could take a toy-brand prequel to a poorly reviewed film and make it his own: it earned about $81.7 million and is widely considered far better than the original. It began Henry Thomas's long run, as Father Tom, and it cast Elizabeth Reaser and Lulu Wilson as mother and daughter two years before Hill House cast them as the same character at different ages. The Lasser Glass hides in the basement, and the screen-used board and planchette came back in Usher's first episode, again beside Wilson.
trivia: Budget of $9 million to $12 million; it grossed $81.7 million worldwide.
The Newton Brothers replaced the first film's composer.
The Lasser Glass appears in a basement corner around the 1:07:00 mark, which Flanagan confirmed on Twitter.
Lin Shaye's post-credits cameo as the older Lina connects it to the 2014 Ouija.
Doug Jones plays the ghoul Marcus under prosthetics.
The board and planchette return in Usher's “A Midnight Dreary,” and Flanagan posted a set photo of himself and Lulu Wilson holding them.

sourceMaterial.author: Stephen King
sourceMaterial.title: Gerald's Game (1992)
sourceMaterial.note: A close adaptation that keeps the eclipse backstory and the Moonlight Man reveal, and gives Jessie's inner voices bodies.

premise: Jessie and Gerald Burlingame drive to an isolated lake house to rescue their marriage. Gerald handcuffs her to the bed for a sex game, they argue, and he dies of a heart attack, leaving her chained with no key and a stray dog working up the nerve to come inside. What follows is mostly one woman on one bed, and Flanagan makes it a crowded film by giving Jessie's inner voices bodies: a smug Gerald and a sharper version of herself argue with her as she dehydrates. Her memories go back to the 1963 solar eclipse and her father's abuse, and at night a tall figure, the Moonlight Man, stands in the corner. She gets free by degloving her own hand, and the epilogue confirms the Moonlight Man was real.
whyItMatters: Gerald's Game is Flanagan's first Stephen King adaptation, of a book long considered unfilmable, and King called the rough cut “hypnotic, horrifying and terrific.” It began the Carla Gugino partnership and paired her with Bruce Greenwood, a duo he reunited in Usher as Verna and Roderick. It carries props from two other films: the headboard is built from the Lasser Glass frame, and Maddie Young's Midnight Mass novel sits on the shelf. Gerald's line “All things serve the Beam” started Flanagan's habit of planting Dark Tower markers in every King project.
trivia: Netflix released it on September 29, 2017.
King called the rough cut “hypnotic, horrifying and terrific.”
The headboard is built from the bottom edge of the Lasser Glass frame; Bruce Larsen designed both.
Jessie grabs a copy of Maddie Young's Midnight Mass from the shelf to throw at the dog.
Gerald says “All things serve the Beam,” a Dark Tower line.
Jessie's abuse happens during the same 1963 eclipse as King's Dolores Claiborne.
Carel Struycken plays the Moonlight Man and returns as Grandpa Flick in Doctor Sleep.

sourceMaterial.author: Shirley Jackson
sourceMaterial.title: The Haunting of Hill House (1959)
sourceMaterial.note: Very loose: names, lines and the opening paragraph come from the novel, while the Crain family drama is Flanagan's invention.

premise: Summer 1992: the Crain family moves into Hill House to renovate and flip it. Something in the house claims the mother, Olivia, and Hugh flees with their five children in the night. Decades later the adult siblings, Steven, Shirley, Theo, Luke and Nell, are each damaged in their own way, and when Nell dies at the house they are pulled back to each other and to it. The series cuts between the two timelines so that every reveal lands in both at once. The Bent-Neck Lady who haunted Nell all her life was Nell herself, at the moment of her death. The Red Room wore a different face for each child. And Hugh stays behind with Olivia so his children can go free.
whyItMatters: Hill House turned Flanagan from a genre filmmaker into a showrunner, and set the template the later Netflix series followed: family trauma, braided timelines, and long monologues about grief. It started the partnerships with Victoria Pedretti, Oliver Jackson-Cohen and Elizabeth Reaser, gave Henry Thomas and Kate Siegel lead roles, and introduced writer Rebecca Leigh Klingel, who invented the Red Room. Its hidden ghosts, dozens per episode by Flanagan's account, set off the fan habit of scrubbing every frame, and the Red Room later gave his production company its name.
trivia: Flanagan directed all ten episodes.
Steven is named for Steven Spielberg, because Amblin brought Flanagan the project; Shirley is named for Shirley Jackson, and her married name, Harris, for Julie Harris of the 1963 film.
Russ Tamblyn, Luke in the 1963 film, plays Dr. Montague.
Hidden-ghost counts vary by outlet: NME lists 33 and IMDb 43.
Bruce Greenwood appears as an uncredited ghost in episode 5, which Flanagan confirmed to Variety.
Writer Rebecca Leigh Klingel came up with the Red Room.
Flanagan has called the series “a 10-hour Oculus.”

episodeNotes.S1E1: Opens on Jackson's famous first paragraph, read as Steven's book, and plants his line that “most times, a ghost is a wish.”
episodeNotes.S1E3: Theo holds a hand in the dark that isn't there, a moment lifted from the novel.
episodeNotes.S1E5: Nell's episode: the final minutes reveal the Bent-Neck Lady is Nell herself, and Bruce Greenwood hides in it as an uncredited ghost.
episodeNotes.S1E6: “Two Storms,” co-written with Jeff Howard, is staged in a handful of long continuous takes and ends with the dead crowding the living.
episodeNotes.S1E10: The Red Room is revealed, Nell delivers the “confetti” speech, and the finale turns Jackson's “walked alone” into “walk together.” Its title comes from the novel's opening paragraph.

sourceMaterial.author: Stephen King
sourceMaterial.title: Doctor Sleep (2013)
sourceMaterial.note: Reconciles the novel with Kubrick's The Shining, returning to the Overlook and giving Dan the boiler ending King wrote for Jack.

premise: Danny Torrance grew up and drank like his father. Getting sober in a small New Hampshire town, he takes work at a hospice and uses his shine to ease the dying, which earns him the nickname Doctor Sleep. Then a girl named Abra Stone, whose shine is far stronger than his, reaches him telepathically. The True Knot, a nomadic cult led by Rose the Hat, survive by feeding on the “steam” of children like her, and they are now hunting Abra. After the Knot kills his friend Billy and Abra's father, Dan takes the fight to the one place with enough ghosts to finish Rose: the derelict Overlook Hotel. He wakes the hotel, lets it consume her, and dies in the boiler fire. Abra later sees his ghost.
whyItMatters: Doctor Sleep is Flanagan's biggest swing: a sequel to both King's novel and Kubrick's The Shining, two works King famously saw differently. His answer was to rebuild the Overlook from Kubrick's own drawings and then give Dan the ending King wrote for Jack. It brought Carl Lumbly and Alex Essoe into the company and gave Robert Longstreet and Katie Parker places in the True Knot. Flanagan got sober while making it, a thread that runs straight into Midnight Mass. The Lasser Glass hangs in the Overlook, and the Dark Tower markers multiplied.
trivia: The Overlook sets were rebuilt from Kubrick's architectural drawings.
Flanagan rejected digital de-aging and impersonation for the Shining roles; Carl Lumbly, Alex Essoe and Henry Thomas took over Hallorann, Wendy and the Jack-faced bartender.
Danny Lloyd, the original Danny, returned for one day after about 38 years away from acting, as a spectator at the baseball game.
Jack Nicholson was reportedly invited to cameo and declined.
On the Lasser Glass, Flanagan said “there was no way I was going to allow the Overlook to be rebuilt without having it on the wall somewhere.”
Flanagan says King called in favors at Sony, which held the Dark Tower rights, to get references such as “Ka is a wheel” into a Warner Bros. film.
The theatrical cut runs 152 minutes; the director's cut runs 180.

sourceMaterial.author: Henry James
sourceMaterial.title: The Turn of the Screw (1898) and other ghost stories
sourceMaterial.note: Loose: the governess, the children and the ghosts come from the novella, while the Lady in the Lake and the love story are new.

premise: 1987: Dani Clayton, a young American au pair, takes a job at Bly Manor in the English countryside, caring for the orphaned Miles and Flora. The house is haunted by the former valet Peter Quint, who has been using Miles's body, and the former governess Rebecca Jessel. Under both is the Lady in the Lake, Viola Willoughby, a 17th-century mistress of the house whose rage has worn away her face and turned Bly into a gravity well that traps the dead. Dani falls for Jamie, the gardener. To save Flora she invites Viola into herself, and she and Jamie get years together before the beast surfaces and Dani drowns herself in Bly's lake. An older Jamie has been telling the whole story at Flora's wedding.
whyItMatters: Bly Manor made the Flanagan company visible as a company: Victoria Pedretti, Oliver Jackson-Cohen, Henry Thomas, Kate Siegel, Katie Parker and Carla Gugino all returned in unrelated roles. It introduced Rahul Kohli and T'Nia Miller, and gave Jamie Flanagan a first staff writing job. Flanagan wrote and directed only the first episode, handing the rest to guest directors including Axelle Carolyn, who has since worked on three of his series. Its faceless ghosts, who lose their features as they forget themselves, are his clearest statement that ghosts are memory.
trivia: Every episode is titled after a Henry James story.
Flanagan wrote and directed only the first episode, “The Great Good Place.”
Most of the faceless Lady in the Lake was performed by stunt performer Daniela Dib, partly because Kate Siegel had a young baby at home.
Flora's dollhouse tracks where the ghosts are; Flanagan called it “our Marauder's Map for this season.”
Flora greets Dani with “You're expected,” the line Olivia uses in Hill House.
Netflix says the series has no story link to Hill House, though many actors return.
Shot at Bridge Studios in Vancouver from September 2019 to February 2020.

episodeNotes.S1E1: “The Great Good Place,” the only episode Flanagan wrote and directed; Flora greets Dani with Olivia Crain's “You're expected.”
episodeNotes.S1E2: “The Pupil,” written by Jamie Flanagan, their first credit as a series writer.
episodeNotes.S1E5: “The Altar of the Dead” follows Hannah Grose slipping between memories until she, and we, learn she has been dead at the bottom of the well since Dani arrived.
episodeNotes.S1E6: “The Jolly Corner,” the most literal James adaptation: Henry Wingrave's double embodies his guilt.
episodeNotes.S1E8: “The Romance of Certain Old Clothes,” directed by Axelle Carolyn, tells Viola and Perdita's story and how the Lady in the Lake began.
episodeNotes.S1E9: “The Beast in the Jungle” gives Dani and Jamie their years together and reveals the Storyteller as the older Jamie.

premise: Riley Flynn comes home to tiny Crockett Island after four years in prison for killing a young woman while driving drunk. The same week, a young priest, Father Paul Hill, arrives to cover for the island's ageing Monsignor Pruitt, and miracles follow: a paralysed girl walks, and elderly parishioners grow young. Father Paul is Pruitt, rejuvenated by a winged creature he met in the Holy Land and believes is an angel. With the zealot Bev Keane, he plans an Easter Vigil where the congregation drinks poisoned wine, dies and rises hungry. Riley, Erin Greene and Sheriff Hassan push back, and the last survivors burn the boats, the church and the houses so that the turned have nowhere to hide from sunrise.
whyItMatters: Midnight Mass is the project Flanagan carried longest and calls his most personal. He drafted it as a novel around 2010, put it on Maddie Young's screen in Hush and on a shelf in Gerald's Game, and got it made only when Netflix, which had once passed, ordered it in 2019. It brought Zach Gilford, Hamish Linklater, Igby Rigney, Matt Biedel, Crystal Balint and Kristin Lehman into the company. Its subjects, faith, addiction and the monologue as confession, are the ones his later work keeps returning to, and Riley is, in his words, “my most thinly veiled avatar for myself.”
trivia: Netflix ordered it in July 2019 after several companies, Netflix among them, had turned it down.
Crockett Island is modelled on Tangier Island, Virginia, where Crockett is the most common surname; Flanagan says it is not a 'Salem's Lot reference.
Flanagan plays the young priest in the Jerusalem flashback in “Book III: Proverbs,” and joined SAG for the part.
Carla Gugino voices the unseen judge who sentences Riley in the first episode.
Alex Essoe's Mildred Gunning goes through five makeup phases as she de-ages, done practically by Fractured FX.
“Book VI: Acts of the Apostles” won the Bram Stoker Award for Superior Achievement in a Screenplay.
The island town was built at Garry Point Park in Richmond, British Columbia.

episodeNotes.S1E1: Riley comes home; Carla Gugino is the unseen judge's voice, and Ed Flynn is reading King's Revival.
episodeNotes.S1E3: Flanagan cameos as the young priest in the Jerusalem flashback, and the Lasser Glass sits half under a sheet on the rec center stage.
episodeNotes.S1E6: The Easter Vigil: the congregation drinks the poisoned wine. The episode won the Bram Stoker Award for screenplay.
episodeNotes.S1E7: The island burns, Erin and Riley give their speeches about what happens when we die, and Warren and Leeza escape.

sourceMaterial.author: Christopher Pike
sourceMaterial.title: The Midnight Club (1994) and other novels
sourceMaterial.note: Fairly loose: the novel supplies the hospice frame, and the stories the teenagers tell adapt other Pike books.

premise: 1994: high school senior Ilonka is diagnosed with terminal thyroid cancer and moves into Brightcliffe, a hospice for young people near Seattle run by Dr. Georgina Stanton. She joins the Midnight Club, residents who meet at midnight to tell each other scary stories, bound by a pact that whoever dies first will send a sign from the other side. Each episode folds one of their tales into the frame, with the cast playing the characters in the stories. Ilonka, meanwhile, digs into the house's past: a cult called the Paragon, and a former patient who reportedly walked out cured. It is a horror series about kids who know exactly how much time they have left, and who spend it keeping each other company.
whyItMatters: The Midnight Club is the Flanaverse's most direct bridge to another writer's whole bibliography: Christopher Pike is an executive producer, and the stories adapt 28 of his books by Flanagan's count. It launched Ruth Codd, Sauriyan Sapkota and Aya Furukawa, who moved straight into Usher with Igby Rigney, and gave Michael Fimognari and first AD Morgan Beggs episodes to direct. Its cancellation after one season, hours after Flanagan and Trevor Macy moved their TV deal to Amazon, left the Flanaverse's great unfinished story; Flanagan published the answers himself.
trivia: Episode 1 holds the Guinness World Record for most scripted jump scares in a single TV episode: 21.
Flanagan, who dislikes jump scares, said he chased the record partly to placate producers who always ask for more.
Netflix cancelled it on December 1, 2022; Flanagan then published his plans for the unanswered questions.
Season 2 would have adapted Christopher Pike's Remember Me.
The Lasser Glass is in the basement junk during the ritual in “Witch,” which Flanagan confirmed.
Ruth Codd, found by the casting team on TikTok, is a below-the-knee amputee like her character, Anya.
A Die Hard poster, Flanagan's favourite film, hangs on a wall for one line.

episodeNotes.S1E1: “The Final Chapter” set the Guinness World Record for most scripted jump scares in a TV episode: 21.
episodeNotes.S1E3: “The Wicked Heart,” directed by Michael Fimognari; Kevin pulls The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger from a locker.
episodeNotes.S1E6: “Witch”: the Lasser Glass is visible in the basement during the ritual.
episodeNotes.S1E7: “Anya,” written by Jamie Flanagan; Flanagan said “Ruth crushes that episode,” and Gugino, Siegel and Linklater voice the TV cop show she watches.
episodeNotes.S1E10: “Midnight,” the finale, directed by longtime first AD Morgan Beggs.

sourceMaterial.author: Edgar Allan Poe
sourceMaterial.title: The Fall of the House of Usher and other tales
sourceMaterial.note: A loose mash-up: Usher is the frame, and each episode builds an heir's death from a different Poe story.

premise: Roderick Usher, head of Fortunato Pharmaceuticals and maker of the opioid Ligodone, loses all six of his children in two weeks. Back at the crumbling house where he grew up, he confesses everything to his old adversary, Assistant US Attorney C. Auguste Dupin. On New Year's Eve 1979, Roderick and his twin sister Madeline made a deal with a woman named Verna: wealth and power for their lifetimes, in exchange for the bloodline ending with them. Each child dies a death styled on a Poe story, from Perry's masquerade to Frederick's pendulum, and Verna is there every time in a different form. It is a dynasty saga in the shape of the Sacklers told as a ghost story, and it ends with the house falling and the line finished.
whyItMatters: Usher is Flanagan's last Netflix series and his grand reunion: Carla Gugino, Bruce Greenwood, Henry Thomas, Kate Siegel, Rahul Kohli, Samantha Sloyan, T'Nia Miller, Zach Gilford, Annabeth Gish, Katie Parker and three Midnight Club teens all return, and Mark Hamill joins. More than any earlier work it is built from callbacks: the Ouija board, the Hush mask, the Lasser Glass and Gerald's Game on a streaming menu. Michael Fimognari directed half the episodes, and its Poe titles continue the habit, begun with Henry James in Bly, of naming episodes after the source.
trivia: Frank Langella was fired mid-shoot in April 2022 after an investigation; Bruce Greenwood replaced him and almost all of Roderick's scenes were reshot.
Verna, never named on screen, is an anagram of “raven.”
Every episode title is a Poe title or line; “A Midnight Dreary” comes from the first line of “The Raven.”
Flanagan directed episodes 1, 2, 5 and 6; Michael Fimognari directed 3, 4, 7 and 8 and shot all eight.
Production designer Laurin Kelsey says the house numbers are always years associated with Poe.
Lenore and Morrie hover over Gerald's Game in a streaming menu in “Goldbug,” an egg Netflix confirmed.
At the ATX TV Festival in 2024, Flanagan said one egg has still gone unfound.

episodeNotes.S1E1: “A Midnight Dreary” takes its title from the first line of “The Raven”; the Ouija board sits in the twins' room, and the Lasser Glass hangs in Verna's 1979 bar.
episodeNotes.S1E2: “The Masque of the Red Death”: Perry's party, a guest in the Hush mask, and a paragraph of Poe's story scrawled on the bathroom wall.
episodeNotes.S1E3: “Murder in the Rue Morgue,” directed by Michael Fimognari: Camille and the chimpanzee from Victorine's lab.
episodeNotes.S1E4: “The Black Cat”: Leo's episode, with the Lasser Glass frame tattooed on his chest.
episodeNotes.S1E5: “The Tell-Tale Heart,” written by Dani Parker, the one episode Flanagan did not write: Victorine and her heart device.
episodeNotes.S1E6: “Goldbug”: Tamerlane's episode, and the Gerald's Game streaming-menu egg.
episodeNotes.S1E7: “The Pit and the Pendulum,” written by Jamie Flanagan: Frederick and the demolition pendulum.
episodeNotes.S1E8: “The Raven,” co-written by Kiele Sanchez: Lenore, Madeline's return, and the house falling into the tarn.

sourceMaterial.author: Stephen King
sourceMaterial.title: “The Life of Chuck,” in If It Bleeds (2020)
sourceMaterial.note: A close adaptation that keeps the novella's reverse three-act structure.

premise: The story runs backward. Act Three: the world is ending. The internet fails, California slides into the sea, the stars go out, and billboards everywhere thank Charles Krantz for “39 great years.” Act Two, nine months earlier: Chuck, an accountant, stops at a street drummer and dances with a stranger, a few minutes of pure joy. Act One: Chuck's orphaned childhood with his grandparents, his discovery of dance, and the locked cupola where his grandfather sees the future. Put back in order, the apocalypse is the universe inside one man, dying with him of a brain tumour. Nick Offerman narrates and Tom Hiddleston plays the adult Chuck. The film contains no horror, and it is Flanagan's warmest work.
whyItMatters: The Life of Chuck is where the Flanaverse's long conversation with death turned openly hopeful, and it won the People's Choice Award at TIFF. It is Flanagan's third King feature and a family affair: his son Cody plays seven-year-old Chuck, and Flanagan appears as a mourner. Mark Hamill, Karen Gillan, Carl Lumbly, Annalise Basso, Heather Langenkamp, Samantha Sloyan, Jacob Tremblay and Kate Siegel are all here. It is also one of the few Flanagan features not shot by Michael Fimognari; Eben Bolter took the camera.
trivia: Won the People's Choice Award at TIFF in September 2024, and the Cheval Noir at Fantasia.
Four actors play Chuck: Cody Flanagan at 7, Benjamin Pajak at 11, Jacob Tremblay at 17 and Tom Hiddleston as an adult.
Rose the Hat's top hat from Doctor Sleep makes a “special, subtle appearance,” per Flanagan; he has not said where.
Flanagan confirmed the Lasser Glass is not in the film.
He says a repeated number, 19, will mean a lot to fans of The Dark Tower.
Darren Aronofsky's Protozoa Pictures optioned the novella first; Flanagan took it over in May 2023.
Shot in Alabama in October and November 2023 under a SAG-AFTRA interim agreement.

sourceMaterial.author: Stephen King
sourceMaterial.title: Carrie (1974)
sourceMaterial.note: The fourth screen version, modernised and expanded, with a new character and the novel's document style used to hint at other telekinetic women.

premise: Carrie White has spent her whole life shut away with her mother, Margaret. When her father Ralph dies, social workers discover the two of them, and Carrie has to attend Thomas Ewen Consolidated High School in Chamberlain as a condition of staying with her mother. Her first period, in the gym shower, sets off both the bullying and the telekinesis, and the eight episodes walk toward the prom from there. Flanagan's version is open-hearted where earlier Carries were guarded: this Carrie is earnest, this Margaret loves her daughter as fiercely as she harms her, and the torment moves onto social media through a “Carrie Red” Instagram account. Police reports, 911 calls and research files, styled like the novel's documents, hint at a wider sisterhood of telekinetic women.
whyItMatters: Carrie is Flanagan's first series for Amazon and his fourth King adaptation. It moves the company into a new house: Samantha Sloyan in a role Flanagan wrote for her, Kate Siegel directing an episode, and Rahul Kohli, Michael Trucco, Ruth Codd and Crystal Balint in the cast. His daughter Theo plays young Margaret. Its LaMerk Industries sign is the latest Dark Tower marker, sharper for the fact that Flanagan first pitched Amazon The Dark Tower and was offered Carrie instead. Renewed in October 2026, it is planned as a trilogy.
trivia: More than 1,400 actresses auditioned for Carrie; Flanagan called it the “most exhaustive and difficult casting experience” of his career.
Flanagan wrote Margaret White for Samantha Sloyan.
Flanagan pitched The Dark Tower to Amazon first; Amazon proposed Carrie.
Flanagan told Gold Derby that “Dark Tower fans are going to love the signage at the place where Ralph White works.”
Mark Hamill opens “Home Economics” under prosthetics as the fake psychic Damon Nostra; his requests were secrecy and a nose.
The cast reunites Battlestar Galactica's Michael Trucco, Katee Sackhoff and Tahmoh Penikett.
Principal Grayle's electrocution at the prom nods to Matthew Lillard's death in Scream, Flanagan told Page Six.
Flanagan's son Rigby sat in the writers' room alongside other teenagers.

episodeNotes.S1E1: “First Period,” written and directed by Flanagan; the LaMerk Industries sign at Ralph White's work site is a confirmed Dark Tower egg.
episodeNotes.S1E5: “Physical Education,” directed by Kyra Sedgwick and written by Elan Gale and Alexandra Magistro.
episodeNotes.S1E6: “Home Economics” opens with Mark Hamill's secret cameo as the fake psychic Damon Nostra.
episodeNotes.S1E7: “Romantic Literature,” written by Jamie Flanagan: the prom, where Principal Grayle's death nods to Matthew Lillard's in Scream.
episodeNotes.S1E8: “AP Physics,” written and directed by Flanagan: Adelaide's “a little bit of shine” nods to Doctor Sleep, and she stops Margaret's heart.

sourceMaterial.author: DC Comics
sourceMaterial.title: Clayface (Matt Hagen)
sourceMaterial.note: An original horror-leaning story built on the DC villain, rewritten for the screen with Hossein Amini.

premise: Matt Hagen climbs from Gotham street kid to Hollywood leading man, and then a crime boss has him disfigured. Abandoned by his team, he turns to the scientist Caitlyn Corr and her experimental treatment, which restores his face and then keeps going, turning him into a shapeshifting creature of clay whose grip on reality starts to slip. Revenge follows. The story is Flanagan's, built around a man whose entire career depends on his face, which is about as close to his own territory as a superhero film gets: body horror as grief for a lost self. He wrote the story and the screenplay with Hossein Amini but did not direct; James Watkins did. DC released it as the third film in its new DC Universe.
whyItMatters: Clayface is the one work on this site Flanagan wrote but did not direct, and a clear view of how his ideas survive other hands. He had wanted to make a horror-leaning Clayface since at least January 2021, and pitched it with Trevor Macy to James Gunn and Peter Safran in March 2023. Scheduling kept him from directing, since The Exorcist and Carrie came first, and by May 2025 he had moved off the project. Gunn has said the story is entirely Flanagan's, and it opened at No. 1 at the US box office.
trivia: Story by Mike Flanagan; screenplay by Flanagan and Hossein Amini.
Flanagan pitched it with Trevor Macy to James Gunn and Peter Safran in March 2023; DC greenlit it in December 2024.
James Watkins was hired to direct by February 2025, and Amini rewrote the script that April and May.
Gunn has said the story is entirely Flanagan's.
Warner Bros. released it on October 23, 2026, after moving it from September 11.
It opened at No. 1 domestically with $24 million.

sourceMaterial.author: The Exorcist franchise
sourceMaterial.title: The Exorcist (1973) and its sequels
sourceMaterial.note: An original new story; Flanagan calls it a “radical new take” and says the earlier films remain canon.

premise: Thirteen years ago, New York detective Julie Miller caught the satanic serial killer known as Father Sunday, and the case made her a hero. Now a new killer has scrawled her name in an altar boy's blood on the wall of a church crypt, and the darkness she thought she had buried with him is coming back, aimed at her 12-year-old son, Max. Priests are drawn in, among them a prison chaplain played by Chiwetel Ejiofor and Laurence Fishburne's Father Nichol. That is most of what Universal has shown so far, through a synopsis and a first teaser. Scarlett Johansson leads, John Leguizamo plays Father Sunday, and Flanagan wrote, directed and edited it, his first feature since The Life of Chuck.
whyItMatters: The Exorcist: Martyrs brings back a long list of the Flanagan company: Rahul Kohli, Hamish Linklater, Carl Lumbly, Samantha Sloyan, Kate Siegel, Carla Gugino, Robert Longstreet, Matt Biedel, John Gallagher Jr. and Benjamin Pajak, with Michael Fimognari shooting and The Newton Brothers scoring. It takes over a franchise after David Gordon Green's planned Believer sequels were cancelled, and it returns Flanagan to the ground of Midnight Mass: faith under pressure, and priests who may not be enough.
trivia: Universal has dated it for March 12, 2027.
Flanagan replaced David Gordon Green's planned Believer sequels in May 2024.
Shot in New York City from March 13 to June 9, 2026.
Flanagan says the “Tubular Bells” theme will not be used.
Earlier dates of April 18, 2025, and March 13, 2026, fell away so Carrie could shoot first.
It is the seventh film in The Exorcist franchise.
The title first surfaced on the Red Room Pictures website in June 2026.
